title: Vayetze: and I knew it not (Genesis 28:16)
hookLine: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not"

cards: The bus stop you stand at every morning. The hallway between the kitchen and the bedroom. The stretch of highway you drive without seeing.
Nobody expects anything holy there. Jacob, running from his brother, comes to an ordinary place as the sun goes down. No town, no inn.
He takes one of the stones lying around, puts it under his head, and lies down on the ground to sleep. Nothing marks the spot.

teach.h: A LADDER FROM EARTH TO HEAVEN.
teach.b: Jacob dreams. A ladder, a sulam, is set up on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and angels of God are going up and coming down on it. Up first, then down, the rabbis noticed.

teach.h: I WILL BE WITH YOU WHEREVER YOU GO.
teach.b: God stands beside him and makes a promise: this land, children like the dust of the earth, and I will be with you and keep you wherever you go, and bring you back.
Jacob wakes up and says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not."
He's afraid, and he says the place is full of awe: nothing less than the house of God, the gate of heaven. He names it Beth-el, house of God.

teach.h: BETH-EL, THAT USED TO BE LUZ.
teach.b: The text adds, almost dryly, that the town used to be called Luz. An ordinary name for an ordinary place. Listen to that line again.
And I knew it not. The Hebrew for I here is anochi, the longer of two Hebrew words for I, and some Hasidic teachers played with it. Why didn't Jacob know God was there?
Because of the anochi: he was full of himself, his fear, his plans, his running.
The rabbis also gave God a name from stories like this: HaMakom, the Place.

teach.h: SURELY THE LORD IS IN THIS PLACE.
teach.b: A midrash says God is the place of the world, but the world is not God's place. There's no spot on earth too plain for it. In Jacob's own words, God was already there; the dream didn't bring him.
What changed was that he woke up and noticed.

how: Jews often call God HaMakom, the Place, and the phrase appears in the traditional words of comfort said to mourners.

o: and he went out, the start of a journey
and he wandered, lost in the desert
and he slept, a night under the stars

games.q: what's inside the dream — tap the pairs.
p: the Place, a name for God

s: Jacob went looking for a holy place to sleep
he stopped at an ordinary spot at sunset and used a stone for a pillow.
the angels in the dream went up first, then came down
the rabbis noticed the order: ascending, then descending.
the text says the town used to be called Luz.

games.q: you wake up on a stone after a dream of angels on a ladder. you're Jacob. what do you say?
o: surely the LORD is in this place, and I knew it not.
I must build a city here.
games.why: Jacob said God was in this place and he hadn't known it, and named it Beth-el, house of God.

practice: Wherever you are right now, the car, a bench, the kitchen floor, look around slowly, as if you'd just woken from Jacob's dream, and find what you've stopped seeing: the light on the wall, the sound of the street, the fact that you're breathing at all.
If you pray, you can say Jacob's line quietly. If not, just let the place be more than it was a minute ago.

wordCard.voice: Vayetze. And he went out: the portion where Jacob sleeps on a stone in nowhere in particular, and wakes up saying God was there all along.

orig.note: Hebrew: and I knew it not. anochi is the long, heavy form of the word I.

carryVoice: Your line: and I knew it not. Beth-el was plain Luz the night before. Day one hundred ninety-two.

sources.q: Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.
